hero.title: Crown Dependencies Observatory
hero.body: Five sections. One argument: the data to understand these islands exists — it's just buried in PDFs. Fiscal flows, demographic trajectories, health system performance, household economics, privacy risk — extracted, visualised, and honest about what the numbers do and don't show.

who.name: James — Isle of Man
paragraphs: The Island punches well below its weight when it comes to understanding itself, starting with its position in the world. Manx first, British second, European third. Its own constitutional position — the overarching authority of Westminster over Manx Government, its fiscal position, precarious; its demographic trajectory, more so; how its health system actually compares; who actually runs this place — and the gap between data that technically exists and data that anyone can use is a problem worth fixing.

James attended Rushen Infants School, where he picked all this up in Mrs Molyneux's class. He later went to the University of Glasgow, where he spent far too much on beer; Imperial College London, where he concluded that nerdiness was an artform; and Warwick Business School for an Executive MBA. All sponsored by either the taxpayer, or the taxpayer via Manx Telecom — so thank you.

Coalfinch is a vehicle for carrying STEM skills into places that don't yet understand what those skills make possible — or what we can do. This observatory is one expression of that — a demonstration that publicly available data, properly extracted and visualised, can inform debate in ways that were simply not accessible before.

Change starts with understanding, and the data to understand these islands exists. James also knows a little about George Akerlof — and rather more about Change Management. Data has a way of destroying established narratives, which is occasionally uncomfortable for the people who depend on them. He is, accordingly, half expecting a hit man.
James also believes that small, distinctive places add something that larger homogenised economies do not. Protecting that takes more than sentiment. It takes understanding the numbers.

This project is still largely one person with too many browser tabs open. A significant amount of the underlying data has been extracted from government PDFs, which is exactly as error-prone as it sounds. If you spot something wrong, the email address is below.
If you have found something wrong, or something missing, please say so.

In Minecraft, there are no canaries — which is a strange omission. The canary in the coal mine is one of the most important data instruments in mining history: a small creature sent into a dangerous place to detect invisible risk, so the miners behind it do not have to find out the hard way.
Minecraft has coal mines. It does not have canaries. So if you want the early warning system, you have to invent the bird. Enter the coalfinch — a made-up creature doing a very real job.

The Isle of Man has a substantial mining history — lead, zinc, and silver at Foxdale and Laxey, worked for centuries, and at its peak one of the most productive lead-mining districts in Britain. No coal, however, as Bishop Wilson recorded as far back as 1726. Whether a Manx miner ever carried a canary is therefore genuinely unclear — though if they did, it would probably have been a local spajjard (sparrow, in a dialect so local it may be specific to Port St Mary, or possibly just a handful of people of a very particular age — spelling approximate). We'll have none of that tropical fanciness here. *author bites into raw turnip*

The name felt right for a project about surfacing risks that are technically visible in public data but practically invisible to the people who should be paying attention to them. Go first. Report back.

sections.label: Economy & Society
sections.desc: Demographics, inflation, unemployment, and productivity. GDP per head, wages, and affordability — what the headline figures show and what they conceal.

sections.label: Government
sections.desc: IoM fiscal flows and departmental budgets, 2016–2025. Public sector employment across all three islands.

sections.label: Households
sections.desc: What residents actually earn, what they pay, and what's left. Includes a household budget tool that produces a shareable Sankey.

sections.label: Health & Care
sections.desc: Manx Care benchmarked against Jersey, Guernsey, and the NHS. Bed capacity modelling for Nobles Hospital.

sections.label: Privacy & Data
sections.desc: Re-identification risk in small populations — the question that started all of this. k-Anonymity explorer and area risk rankings.

dataQuality: Everything here is sourced from public documents — government accounts, census publications, statistical bulletins. Where data is estimated, projected, or has known quality issues, that is flagged inline.
